introduction: As Athens prepares to celebrate the marriage of Theseus and Hippolyta, Hermia faces punishment for refusing the husband her father has chosen. Her plan to escape with Lysander draws two other lovers into a nearby wood, where a quarrel between the fairy rulers is already disturbing the natural world. A group of craftsmen also chooses the wood to rehearse a wedding entertainment. Their paths cross under the influence of Puck, whose magic changes what people see and whom they believe they love.

fullSynopsis.text: Egeus asks Theseus to enforce his authority over Hermia, who loves Lysander instead of her father's choice, Demetrius. Theseus gives her until his own wedding to accept Demetrius, die or vow lifelong chastity. Lysander proposes escaping to his aunt's house beyond Athenian jurisdiction. They tell Helena their plan, and she decides to reveal it to Demetrius, hoping to earn his gratitude even though he has abandoned her for Hermia. In another part of Athens, Quince assembles craftsmen to perform Pyramus and Thisbe at the wedding. Bottom wants several parts, but Quince assigns him the leading lover and arranges a woodland rehearsal.

In the wood, Oberon and Titania quarrel over an Indian boy whom Titania is raising for his dead mother's sake. She attributes floods, blighted crops and confused seasons to their discord. Oberon sends Puck for a flower whose juice makes sleepers love the next creature they see. He intends to humiliate Titania until she yields the boy. After overhearing Demetrius cruelly reject Helena, he also orders Puck to charm the Athenian man into loving her. Oberon anoints Titania himself. Puck mistakes the sleeping Lysander for Demetrius, and Lysander wakes to Helena, abandons Hermia and pursues his new love.

The craftsmen rehearse near Titania's sleeping place, discussing how to explain the lion, sword, moonlight and wall so that their audience will not be frightened or confused. Puck gives Bottom an ass's head, scattering his terrified companions. Bottom stays and sings, waking Titania. Under the spell, she adores him and orders her fairies to attend him. Puck reports his joke to Oberon, but their satisfaction is interrupted by Demetrius and Hermia. Seeing the real Demetrius, Oberon realizes that Puck has charmed the wrong man. He sends Puck to fetch Helena and applies the flower to Demetrius's eyes himself.

Demetrius wakes loving Helena, so both men now compete for the woman whom neither had previously pursued that night. Helena believes that they and Hermia have combined to mock her. Hermia, bewildered by Lysander's rejection, accuses Helena of stealing him. Their friendship dissolves into insults and threatened violence, while the men leave to fight. Oberon orders Puck to prevent the duel and undo Lysander's enchantment. By imitating each rival's voice, Puck leads them separately through the darkness until they tire and sleep. The women also lie down nearby. Puck applies the remedy to Lysander, to restore his earlier attachment to Hermia.

Oberon reports that Titania has surrendered the boy during her enchantment. He releases her, has Puck remove Bottom's ass's head and reconciles with her. Theseus, Hippolyta and Egeus discover the sleeping lovers. Demetrius, whose charm remains in place, declares that he now loves Helena. Theseus overrules Egeus and orders both couples married alongside himself and Hippolyta. The lovers leave uncertain how to distinguish the night's events from dreams. Bottom wakes with an experience he cannot describe and imagines a ballad about it. His return to the anxious craftsmen rescues their entertainment, while news from the temple confirms the additional marriages.

At the wedding festivities, Theseus chooses the craftsmen's play despite warnings about its quality. The courtiers joke as the performers explain their roles and enact a fatal misunderstanding: Pyramus kills himself after finding Thisbe's bloodied mantle, and Thisbe kills herself on discovering him. Bottom then offers a dance instead of an epilogue. After the mortals retire, Oberon and Titania lead their fairies in blessing the house and its newly married couples, promising faithful love and fortunate children. Puck addresses the audience directly, asking them to regard the performance as a dream if it has offended and to show friendship with applause.

acts.label: ACT I
acts.summary: Theseus and Hippolyta anticipate their wedding, but Egeus interrupts with a demand that Hermia marry Demetrius instead of Lysander. Theseus presents her alternatives as obedience, death or lifelong chastity, allowing her time until the wedding to decide. Lysander and Hermia arrange to flee through the wood to his aunt's home, where Athenian law cannot reach them. They confide in Helena, who remains devoted to Demetrius despite his preference for Hermia. Helena decides to reveal the escape so that she can see him as he pursues them. Meanwhile Quince assigns parts for a wedding play. Bottom's eagerness to act several roles complicates the preparations, and the craftsmen agree to rehearse secretly in the same wood.

acts.label: ACT II
acts.summary: Oberon and Titania's dispute over her Indian attendant has divided the fairy court; Titania describes the destructive weather and disordered seasons their quarrel has produced. Oberon obtains a magical flower to make her love an unsuitable creature and surrender the child. Overhearing Helena plead with the hostile Demetrius, he tells Puck to use the flower on the Athenian man as well. Titania's fairies sing her to sleep, after which Oberon puts the juice on her eyelids. Lysander and Hermia lose their way and sleep apart. Puck mistakes their separation for evidence that Lysander is Helena's cruel lover and charms him. Helena wakes him, and he follows her in sudden devotion, leaving Hermia to wake alone from a frightening dream.

acts.label: ACT III
acts.summary: The craftsmen rehearse their tragedy, planning explanations to reassure the audience that its dangers are imaginary. Puck transforms Bottom's head into an ass's, frightening away his companions. Bottom's song wakes Titania, whose enchantment makes her love him and summon fairies to serve him. Oberon discovers Puck's mistaken treatment of Lysander and charms Demetrius himself. Both men now pursue Helena, who believes their declarations are a conspiracy of mockery. Hermia accuses Helena of taking Lysander, and the women quarrel while the men challenge one another. Oberon orders Puck to separate the rivals and restore Lysander. Puck impersonates their voices until they fall asleep, then applies the antidote as all four lovers rest in the wood.

acts.label: ACT IV
acts.summary: Titania pampers Bottom while Oberon explains that she has given him the Indian boy. He ends her enchantment, orders Bottom restored and renews their harmony. Theseus's hunting party finds the four sleeping lovers. Egeus again demands punishment, but Demetrius declares his love for Helena, and Theseus overrides the father's objections. He directs both young couples to marry in the temple with himself and Hippolyta. The lovers follow, still unsure whether the night's events were dreams. Bottom wakes separately, unable to put his extraordinary experience into words, and proposes having Quince make a ballad of it. The other craftsmen despair of performing without him until he reappears and rallies them to prepare for the palace entertainment.

acts.label: ACT V
acts.summary: Theseus doubts the lovers' account of the wood, while Hippolyta finds significance in their shared experience. He selects the craftsmen's Pyramus and Thisbe for the wedding entertainment despite Philostrate's objections. Their awkward prologue, talking wall, explanatory lion and moon provoke running commentary from the noble audience. Within the play, a bloodied mantle persuades Pyramus that Thisbe is dead; his suicide leads to hers. The performers finish with a dance, and the married company retires. Puck prepares the house for the returning fairies. Oberon and Titania bless the couples and their future children through song and dance. Finally Puck turns outward to the audience, offering the whole performance as a dream and asking for applause and goodwill.
